analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover prescription drugs to cover prescription contraceptives equally.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House bill requiring insurance coverage of prescription contraceptives drew 141 cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote, dying when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred group and individual health plans from excluding prescription contraceptives if they cover other prescription drugs and services. It also would have stopped plans from penalizing doctors who prescribe contraception or rewarding doctors who withhold it. Plans could still charge normal copays and deductibles, just no higher for contraception than for comparable drugs and services.
analysis.who_benefits: Women with private health insurance — about three-quarters of women of childbearing age rely on some form of private coverage — who currently pay full out-of-pocket costs for contraceptives that many plans cover for every other kind of prescription drug. The bill's findings note half of indemnity plans and only 7 percent of HMOs covered any non-sterilization contraceptive method, and that women of reproductive age spend 68 percent more than men out of pocket.

how_it_helps.text: Plans that cover other outpatient prescription drugs and services could no longer exclude or restrict prescription contraceptive drugs, devices, and outpatient contraceptive services [S2] [S3].
Plans could not deny enrollment or renewal because of someone's use or potential use of contraceptives, and could not offer individuals cash to accept weaker coverage [S2] [S3].
Plans could not reduce a doctor's reimbursement for prescribing contraception or reward doctors for withholding it [S2] [S3].
The same rules applied to individual-market policies, not just employer plans, and took effect for plan years starting on or after January 1, 2000 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group health plans, who would cover a benefit many had excluded; costs would partly flow into premiums shared by all enrollees. The bill allowed cost-sharing but only up to what plans charge for comparable drugs and services [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises covered benefits without directly paying for them, so some of the cost would surface in premiums paid by all enrollees, including people who will never use contraception [S3].

Plans could still impose deductibles, coinsurance, and limits on contraceptives — just no heavier than for comparable drugs and services — so women would keep paying meaningful cost-sharing for care they need [S3].

The bill contained no religious or moral exemption for plans or employers, a significant objection for those who object to subsidizing contraception, and it applied to the individual market as well as employer plans [S2] [S3].
It covered only FDA-approved prescription methods and equivalent outpatient services, not non-prescription contraceptives [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: expanded contraceptive coverage for millions of insured women, partly financed by premiums spread across all enrollees and by insurers giving up a cost-saving exclusion. The bill's own findings argue contraceptives are cost-effective — that every dollar invested in family planning saves four to fourteen dollars in pregnancy and health care costs — and that reducing unintended pregnancy reduces the need for abortion [S3]. The design is narrow: it mandates parity, not free coverage, and leaves standard cost-sharing in place [S3]. The strongest objection is the lack of any conscience exemption, which was a live political concern for a mandate of this kind [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to two committees, which passed it down to subcommittees in July 1999; it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Greenwood (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 10, 1999, with 25 original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
It was referred to both the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
In July 1999 it was referred to the Health and Environment Subcommittee and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, where it sat [S5].
The bill attracted 141 cosponsors — 125 Democrats, 15 Republicans, and 1 Independent — roughly a third of the House, but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it [S4] [S5].
No further action was recorded after the subcommittee referrals; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans were better off: they kept the ability to exclude contraceptive coverage, and women continued paying the full out-of-pocket cost of prescription contraception for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

for.name: Rep. James C. Greenwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of 25 original cosponsors, including both Republicans and Democrats such as Mrs. Lowey, Mr. Waxman, and Mrs. Morella

for.name: 15 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the coalition explicitly bipartisan from introduction

against.name: Rep. Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; after subcommittee referral in July 1999, the Commerce side took no recorded action [S5]

against.name: Rep. William F. Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; after subcommittee referral in July 1999, the Education and Workforce side took no recorded action [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan in ratio if not in raw count: 125 of 141 cosponsors were Democrats, but Republicans sponsored the bill and 15 Republicans joined, and the bill made no headway in either committee despite majority-Republican House control.

industries.note: Insurers had been excluding or restricting contraceptive coverage while covering other prescription drugs — the bill's findings note only 7 percent of HMOs covered any non-sterilization method — and the bill would have ended that exclusion in both group and individual markets. The bill never passed, so insurers kept the exclusion and the savings it produced.

Employers would have financed a new covered benefit for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2000, though the bill's findings argue the benefit is cost-effective by reducing unintended pregnancy costs. Employers were not named in the record as taking a position, so their opposition is not documented here.
